Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Roman.
Friday's aviation ground stop kept thousands of travelers stranded for hours, only to be told their flight was canceled.
Yvette Fernandez talked with travelers in Phoenix who missed connecting flights to dream vacations, cruises and more.
Nancy Villegas and her best friend planned to travel from Phoenix to Las Vegas to meet with friends for a Raiders game.
The typically easy one-hour flight turned into hours of delays with few updates.
They knew all along that this flight was going to get canceled and they didn't have the staff for it since the cancellation started since yesterday.
Flight crews were also delayed. Villegas said it became increasingly frustrating to see one pilot and one crew member waiting to work their flight.
But two were not enough to meet FAA crew requirements. When the flight cancellation was announced, Villegas and her friend along with two others headed in the same destination went from stranded strangers to travel buddies as they decided to drive overnight.
For NPR News, I'm Yvette Fernandez in Phoenix.
The National Transportation Safety Board says Friday's collision on the Mississippi River at the port of New Orleans was caused by a failed steering mechanism on an asphalt tanker that slammed into a docked cruise ship.
The NTSB's Bart Barnum is the senior investigator in charge for marine safety. He briefed reporters.
The Atlantic asphalt was upbound on the Mississippi River in the proximity of the Crescent City Connection Bridge.
It experienced a steering casualty resulting in the rudder remaining to starboard.
Many of the more than 180 people on board the ship were tossed into the Mississippi when it listed and then capsized. 32 suffered minor injuries.
At Sunday's briefing, the NTSB did not say it would cause the steering mechanism failure.
On Wall Street, investors are keeping an eye on NVIDIA. They'll be looking this week at its former CEO scandals and towards the chipmaker's earnings.
NPR's Stephen Bishasha reports.
There has been a pattern over the past few years on the AI side of the stock market.
Investors get worried the industry is overvalued. Then, NVIDIA shares another quarter of jaw-dropping earnings beating Wall Street expectations.
Tuesday, NVIDIA will again report its latest earnings during an especially tough time for the industry and the company.
The tech-heavy NASDAQ is down about 7.5% over the month.
NVIDIA's stock value has also fallen sharply after the ouster of its scandal-plagued CEO Jensen Wong last week.
Anthropic is looking to join that shaky stock market with an initial public offering planned for later this week.
The price Anthropic's currently signaling would value the company at $1.4 trillion.
Stephen Bishasha, NPR News.
Tyson's food Walmart and Target will also announce earnings this week. It's NPR.
A nearly 100-year-old Georgia O'Keeffe painting that was found in New York City is going up for auction this week.
NPR's Chandelice Duster has more.
The painting from 1930 that has been buried in a New York City closet for decades will go up for auction on Tuesday.
The family of the woman who owned the painting said they believe it was a graduation gift from the 1960s.
The long-lost O'Keeffe works shows a New Mexico landscape with hills and earth-toned colors.
It has been on display at Christie's in New York since early November.
Tylee Abbott, senior specialist and international director of American art at Christie's,
said in a statement that finding a painting by such an acclaimed artist is "a once-in-a-lifetime moment."
The painting is estimated to sell for more than $3 million at Christie's during the auction.
Chandelice Duster, NPR News.
Four National Football League referees Sunday pulled double duty.
They worked two games in two different cities because of Friday's nationwide FAA grounding and the resulting transportation challenges.
The four, including Crew Chief Don Willard, officiated the 1PM Miami Dolphins vs. Indianapolis Colts game in Indianapolis.
After the game, they drove 110 miles in about two hours to Cincinnati to officiate the late game, the Bengals vs. the Pittsburgh Steelers.
The head of the union representing the NFL officials called the travel difficulties "a unique, unprecedented situation that required our officials to make adjustments."
Several college games were also rescheduled.
I'm Dan Roman, NPR.
